issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, although the required substance may be conveyed without using exact formulaic words.
material_facts: The plaintiff did not expressly plead readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.

The plaint stated only that he had asked the agent to arrange execution of the sale deed, without identifying when the demand was made; no demand or tender was made to the owner within the contractual period.
The plaintiff served notice only on the agent after that period had expired and after learning that the property had been sold to another purchaser; the owner did not receive notice.
The plaintiff's testimony that he was then ready to pay the balance did not establish that he had been ready and willing throughout the relevant period.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff had not substantially complied with the requirements for specific performance, and could not obtain that relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires both an averment and proof that the plaintiff has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms required of him. Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to the Code of Civil Procedure indicate the required pleadings. Exact words are not indispensable where the pleadings as a whole and the evidence at trial show readiness and willingness in substance, but a bare plea is insufficient without proof. The Court relied on Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley, Abdul Khader Rowther v. P.K. Sara Bai, Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi, and Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.no_substantive_readiness_pleading: The plaintiff's pleadings, read as a whole, do not convey that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform the essential terms required of the plaintiff.
predicates.no_proof_of_continuous_readiness: The evidence does not establish that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform those terms throughout the relevant period.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance plaintiff neither pleads readiness and willingness in substance nor proves it, the rule's output is denial of specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking discretionary specific performance must approach the court within a reasonable time, assessed in light of the contract and all surrounding circumstances, even when time is not of the essence.
material_facts: The agreement allowed three years for execution of the sale deed, but the plaintiff produced no material showing that he asked the owner to execute it or tendered the balance consideration during that period.
The plaintiff's notice was sent only after the contractual period had expired and after he learned that the owner had transferred the property to another purchaser.
The plaintiff filed suit almost six years after entering the agreement.
issues.conclusion: Having regard to the delay and the plaintiff's conduct, he was not entitled to the discretionary relief of specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Even where time is not of the essence, a plaintiff must perform within a reasonable time, determined from the express terms of the contract, the nature of the property, and the surrounding circumstances. Specific performance is discretionary and equitable relief, and the plaintiff's conduct is relevant to whether it should be granted. The Court relied on Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, Veerayee Ammal v. Seeni Ammal, and Lourdu Mari David v. Louis Chinnaya Arogiaswamy.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.performance_sought_only_after_reasonable: The plaintiff sought contractual performance only after a period that was unreasonable in light of the contract and surrounding circumstances.
predicates.no_timely_approach_to_contracting_owner: The plaintiff did not timely ask the owner or other person able to perform the contract to complete it.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance plaintiff delays beyond a reasonable time and does not timely approach the person able to perform, the rule's output is denial of equitable specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not overturn a lower court's refusal of discretionary equitable relief merely because it might have exercised its discretion differently; interference requires a demonstrated error in the exercise of discretion.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both refused discretionary specific-performance relief.
The High Court reversed those decisions without finding that the lower courts had exercised their discretion on a wrong legal principle.
The Supreme Court found no basis for that interference with the lower courts' discretionary decisions.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have interfered with the lower courts' refusal of discretionary relief, and its judgment could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court ordinarily should not substitute its own exercise of discretion for that of the lower court when the discretion was exercised reasonably and judicially. Interference is justified where the lower court acted unreasonably or capriciously, ignored relevant facts, or otherwise exercised discretion on a wrong legal principle. The Court relied on Uttar Pradesh Co-operative Federation Ltd. v. Sunder Bros. and Lalit Kumar Jain v. Jaipur Traders Corporation Pvt. Ltd.

predicates.appeal_from_discretionary_refusal: The proceeding is an appeal from a lower court's refusal to grant discretionary equitable relief.
predicates.lower_courts_refused_equitable_relief: The lower courts refused the requested equitable relief in the exercise of their discretion.
predicates.higher_court_reversed_without_finding_di: A higher court reversed that refusal without finding that the lower courts exercised their discretion unreasonably, capriciously, or on a wrong legal principle, or ignored relevant facts.

issues.definition: When lower courts have refused equitable relief in their discretion and a higher court reverses without identifying an error in that exercise, the rule's output is that appellate interference is unjustified.
